claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is initially a single-phase BCC solid solution.
Atomic-size and modulus mismatches produce inherent lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Random mixing in single-phase refractory high-entropy alloys creates local fluctuations and lattice distortions that impede dislocation motion.
Differential thermal contraction among local compositional regions or phases generates internal residual stresses during cooling or composite solidification.
Substantial thermal-expansion mismatch can exist among locally distinct regions of nominally single-phase HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal-mismatch residual stresses interact with pre-existing lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
The interaction between residual stress and lattice distortion alters dislocation mobility.
The interaction between residual stress and lattice distortion alters the Peierls barrier.
Residual-stress-mediated changes in dislocation mobility govern the tensile-creep behavior of HfNbTaTiZr at 1250 °C.
Residual-stress-mediated changes in dislocation mobility govern microhardness after cold rolling.
Thermal-mismatch residual stresses modify the temperature dependence of the elastic moduli between 293 and 1100 K.
Thermal-mismatch residual stresses influence aging-induced hardening between 600 and 800 °C.
An intermediate annealing or buffering step can homogenize thermal-expansion properties and reduce internal residual stresses.
Reducing residual stresses will decrease high-temperature yield strength or resistance to tensile creep relative to conventionally processed samples.
Greater thermal mismatch will produce higher yield stresses through increased dislocation pinning by residual stresses.
Greater thermal mismatch will enhance microhardening through increased dislocation pinning by residual stresses.
The proposed mechanism is most relevant from approximately 600 to 1250 °C while the alloy remains single-phase BCC.
If additional phases form or the stated temperature bounds are exceeded, other mechanisms may dominate.
Solid-solution strengthening is commonly dominant in single-phase refractory high-entropy alloys.
The cited evidence supports thermal-expansion effects in similar high-entropy alloys.
